description: A broad-spectrum Class III antiarrhythmic with electrophysiologic properties spanning all four Vaughan Williams classes, widely used for refractory ventricular and supraventricular arrhythmias.
mechanism_of_action: Predominantly blocks myocardial outward potassium currents (IKr, IKs), prolonging action potential duration and refractory period; additionally blocks inactivated sodium channels (Class I), non-competitively blocks beta receptors (Class II), and inhibits L-type calcium channels (Class IV).
pharmacodynamics: Suppresses ectopic ventricular and supraventricular pacemakers, slows sinus rate and AV nodal conduction, and terminates re-entrant tachycardias; minimal negative inotropy allows safe use in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.
absorption: Slow and erratic oral absorption (30-50%); high-fat meals increase absorption by 2- to 3-fold; peak plasma concentration in 3 to 7 hours.
distribution: Enormous volume of distribution (approx. 60 L/kg); accumulates extensively in adipose tissue, lungs, liver, and skin; 96% bound to plasma albumin.
metabolism: Extensively metabolized in the liver by CYP3A4 and CYP2C8 to active desethylamiodarone (DEA); undergoes enterohepatic recycling.
excretion: Excreted predominantly in bile and faeces via hepatic elimination; urinary excretion of parent drug is negligible (<1%).
half_life: 26 to 107 days (mean terminal elimination half-life approx. 50 days; tissue effects persist for months post-discontinuation)
onset: Oral: 2 to 3 days (with loading dose); IV: within hours
indications: Recurrent ventricular fibrillation (VF) and hemodynamically unstable ventricular tachycardia (VT) refractory to other therapy
Advanced cardiac life support (ACLS) in pulseless VT/VF cardiac arrest
Maintenance of sinus rhythm in symptomatic atrial fibrillation (especially with heart failure or left ventricular hypertrophy)
contraindications: Severe sinus node dysfunction causing marked sinus bradycardia
Second- or third-degree AV block without a functioning pacemaker
Cardiogenic shock
Known hypersensitivity to amiodarone or iodine (contains 37% iodine by weight)
warnings: Black box warning: Fatal pulmonary toxicity (hypersensitivity pneumonitis or alveolar fibrosis in up to 10-17% on chronic high doses)
Hepatotoxicity: elevated serum transaminases and fulminant cirrhosis
Thyroid dysfunction: iodine-induced hypothyroidism (common, treatable with levothyroxine) or hyperthyroidism (AIT type 1 or 2)
Corneal microdeposits (present in virtually 100% on chronic therapy) and optic neuropathy/blindness
Skin blue-gray slate pigmentation (ceruloderma) on sun-exposed areas
common_adverse_effects: Corneal microdeposits (benign vortex keratopathy in almost all patients)
serious_adverse_effects: Severe symptomatic bradycardia / complete AV block
drug_interactions: Warfarin (potent CYP2C9 inhibition doubles INR; immediately reduce warfarin dose by 33-50%)
Digoxin (P-glycoprotein inhibition doubles serum digoxin levels; halve digoxin dose)
Statins (simvastatin/atorvastatin - risk of severe rhabdomyolysis; cap simvastatin at 20 mg)
QT-prolonging drugs (macrolides, fluoroquinolones - additive QT risk)
monitoring: Baseline and annual chest X-ray and pulmonary function tests (PFTs including DLCO)
Baseline and every 6-month thyroid function tests (TSH, free T4)
Baseline and every 6-month liver function tests (AST, ALT, alkaline phosphatase)
Annual ophthalmologic examination (slit lamp and fundoscopy)
Continuous ECG during IV infusion; 12-lead ECG every 3-6 months
pregnancy: Category D; strictly avoided in pregnancy unless life-threatening arrhythmias (causes fetal hypothyroidism, goiter, and growth restriction).
lactation: Excreted in significant quantities in breast milk; breastfeeding is strictly contraindicated.
pediatric: Weight-adjusted dosing in pediatric resuscitation (5 mg/kg IV bolus in cardiac arrest).
geriatric: Elderly patients are at heightened risk of pulmonary fibrosis, thyroid toxicity, and severe bradycardia; use the lowest effective maintenance dose (100-200 mg daily).
renal: No dosage adjustment required in renal impairment or hemodialysis (negligible renal clearance).
hepatic: Close monitoring and dose reduction recommended in severe hepatic disease (primary elimination organ).
advantages: Most effective antiarrhythmic for suppressing ventricular tachycardia and maintaining sinus rhythm in atrial fibrillation
Safe in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (does not worsen cardiac mortality, unlike Class I antiarrhythmics)
First-line ACLS medication for shock-refractory pulseless VT/VF
disadvantages: Severe multiorgan toxicities (lungs, liver, thyroid, eyes, skin) requiring lifelong monitoring
Extremely long 50-day half-life means side effects and drug interactions persist for months after stopping
key_points: Halve digoxin and warfarin doses immediately when starting amiodarone
Requires regular checks of thyroid function, liver enzymes, and chest X-rays due to iodine accumulation
memory_trick: AMIODARONE: Action spans all classes; Massive volume of distribution; Iodine overload (thyroid); Organ toxicities (lung/liver); Decreases Warfarin dose.

description: A potent Class IC antiarrhythmic with marked sodium channel blockade and slow dissociation kinetics, used as the first-line 'pill-in-the-pocket' for paroxysmal atrial fibrillation in structurally normal hearts.
mechanism_of_action: Markedly blocks open fast inward voltage-gated sodium channels (Nav1.5) with slow dissociation kinetics; significantly slows phase 0 depolarization and His-Purkinje conduction velocity; also blocks cardiac ryanodine receptor (RyR2), suppressing spontaneous calcium release from sarcoplasmic reticulum.
pharmacodynamics: Produces marked prolongation of PR and QRS intervals with minimal effect on action potential duration (APD) or QTc; terminates and prevents supraventricular and catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardias (CPVT).
absorption: Rapidly and almost completely absorbed (approx. 90-95%); peak plasma concentrations in 2 to 3 hours; food does not impair absorption.
distribution: Apparent volume of distribution approx. 8 to 10 L/kg; 40% bound to plasma proteins.
metabolism: Metabolized in the liver by CYP2D6 to meta-O-dealkylated flecainide and its lactam metabolite (minor activity); subject to genetic polymorphism.
excretion: Eliminated equally by renal excretion of unchanged drug (approx. 30-40%) and urinary excretion of hepatic metabolites; excretion decreases in alkaline urine.
half_life: 12 to 20 hours (mean 14 hours; extended up to 30 hours in renal failure or severe heart failure)
indications: Maintenance of normal sinus rhythm in paroxysmal atrial fibrillation or flutter in STRUCTURALLY NORMAL HEARTS
Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardias (AVNRT, AVRT / Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome)
Pill-in-the-pocket acute termination of recent-onset atrial fibrillation (200-300 mg single oral dose)
Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (CPVT) refractory to beta-blockers
contraindications: STRUCTURAL HEART DISEASE (prior myocardial infarction, coronary artery disease, heart failure with reduced or preserved EF - CAST trial: 2.5x increase in cardiac mortality)
Preexisting second- or third-degree AV block or bifascicular block without pacemaker
Cardiogenic shock
Concurrent use of other Class I antiarrhythmics
warnings: Black box warning: STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED in patients with prior myocardial infarction or structural heart disease (CAST trial demonstrated increased mortality from lethal ventricular proarrhythmia)

Atrial flutter: flecainide can slow atrial flutter rate to 200 bpm allowing 1:1 AV conduction and life-threatening ventricular rates of 200 bpm (ALWAYS co-administer an AV nodal blocker like a beta-blocker or verapamil)
Narrow therapeutic index: monitor plasma levels (0.2 to 1.0 mcg/mL)
common_adverse_effects: Visual disturbances (blurred vision, difficulty focusing, spots before eyes)
serious_adverse_effects: Lethal ventricular proarrhythmia / polymorphic VT (in ischemic or scarred myocardium)
1:1 AV conduction in atrial flutter with hemodynamic collapse
Sinus arrest or severe heart block
drug_interactions: CYP2D6 inhibitors (fluoxetine, paroxetine, quinidine - elevate flecainide to toxic proarrhythmic levels)
Amiodarone (doubles flecainide levels; cut flecainide dose by 50%)
Digoxin and beta-blockers (additive negative dromotropy; flecainide increases digoxin levels by 15-25%)
monitoring: Baseline 12-lead ECG: verify QRS duration (<120 ms) and check for Q-waves or ischemia
Pre-treatment echocardiogram or stress test: RULE OUT coronary artery disease and heart failure
Trough serum flecainide levels (therapeutic range: 0.2 to 1.0 mcg/mL; toxicity > 1.0 mcg/mL)
Renal function tests (BUN and serum creatinine)
pregnancy: Category C; use only if potential benefit justifies potential risk.
lactation: Excreted in high concentrations in breast milk; breastfeeding not recommended.
pediatric: Approved in pediatric patients for refractory SVT and CPVT (dosed by body surface area: 50-100 mg/m2/day).
geriatric: Age-related decline in renal clearance increases toxicity risk; start with 50 mg twice daily.
renal: Strict dose reduction required if CrCl < 35 mL/min: start with 50 mg every 12 to 24 hours; monitor plasma levels closely.
hepatic: Dose reduction required in severe hepatic impairment; monitor plasma levels.
advantages: Gold standard oral 'pill-in-the-pocket' for terminating paroxysmal atrial fibrillation outside the hospital
Exceptional efficacy in terminating and preventing AVNRT, AVRT, and Wolff-Parkinson-White arrhythmias in healthy hearts
Unique RyR2 receptor inhibition makes it life-saving in CPVT
disadvantages: LETHAL in patients with heart disease, previous heart attacks, or heart failure (CAST trial)
Can trigger 1:1 atrial flutter with rapid ventricular rates unless combined with a beta-blocker
key_points: CRITICAL RULE: Safe ONLY in structurally normal hearts (NO prior heart attack, CAD, or heart failure)
Always prescribe a beta-blocker with flecainide to prevent dangerous 1:1 heart racing in atrial flutter
memory_trick: FLECA-inide: First Line for structurally Empty Cardiac Anatomy (normal hearts only); Avoid in Ischemia/infarct (CAST trial).

description: A Class IC antiarrhythmic with intrinsic mild beta-blocking and local anesthetic properties, used for maintaining sinus rhythm in atrial fibrillation and supraventricular tachycardias.
mechanism_of_action: Blocks fast inward sodium channels (Class IC) with slow recovery kinetics, slowing phase 0 depolarization; structurally similar to propranolol, exerting mild non-selective beta-adrenergic blockade (approx. 1/40th the potency of propranolol).
pharmacodynamics: Slows intraventricular and AV nodal conduction, prolongs PR and QRS intervals, suppresses ectopic atrial triggers, and prevents re-entrant tachycardias; mild beta-blocking action helps prevent 1:1 AV conduction in atrial flutter.
absorption: Rapidly and completely absorbed (>95%); undergoes extensive saturable (non-linear) hepatic first-pass metabolism; bioavailability ranges from 5% to 50% depending on CYP2D6 metabolizer status; take with food to improve absorption.
distribution: Widely distributed; apparent volume of distribution approx. 2 to 4 L/kg; 97% bound to plasma alpha-1 acid glycoprotein.
metabolism: Extensively metabolized in the liver by CYP2D6 to active 5-hydroxypropafenone (which possesses equal sodium-blocking activity and less beta-blocking activity) and by CYP3A4 to N-depropylpropafenone.
excretion: Excreted in faeces (approx. 53% via biliary route) and urine (approx. 38% as glucuronide and sulfate metabolites); less than 1% unchanged drug in urine.
half_life: Extensive metabolizers: 2 to 10 hours; Poor metabolizers: 10 to 32 hours
duration: 8 hours (IR tablet dosed TID); 12 hours (SR capsule dosed BID)
indications: Maintenance of sinus rhythm in patients with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation/flutter in the absence of structural heart disease
Prevention of paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardias (PSVT), AVNRT, and AVRT
'Pill-in-the-pocket' conversion of recent-onset atrial fibrillation (450-600 mg single oral dose)
contraindications: Structural heart disease (coronary artery disease, previous myocardial infarction, reduced left ventricular ejection fraction)
Severe bronchospasm, asthma, or severe COPD (due to intrinsic beta-blocking activity)
Severe bradycardia, sick sinus syndrome, or second/third-degree AV block without pacemaker
Cardiogenic shock or severe hypotension
warnings: Black box warning: CONTRAINDICATED in structural heart disease (Class IC proarrhythmia risk as demonstrated in the CAST trial)
Non-linear pharmacokinetics: doubling the dose can increase serum drug concentrations by 300%
Intrinsic beta-blocker effect can trigger acute asthma attacks or worsen heart failure
common_adverse_effects: Metallic or bitter taste (characteristic side effect in up to 15-20%)
serious_adverse_effects: Complete AV heart block / sinus arrest
drug_interactions: CYP2D6 inhibitors (fluoxetine, paroxetine - substantially increase propafenone levels and beta-blockade)
Warfarin (propafenone inhibits warfarin metabolism, increasing INR; reduce warfarin dose)
Digoxin (increases serum digoxin levels by 35-85%; reduce digoxin dose)
CYP3A4 inhibitors/inducers
monitoring: Baseline 12-lead ECG (monitor PR and QRS prolongation; discontinue if QRS widens >25% over baseline)
Baseline echocardiogram: strictly exclude ischemic heart disease and ventricular dysfunction
Liver function tests and complete blood count
pregnancy: Category C; use during pregnancy only if potential benefit justifies potential risk.
lactation: Excreted in human milk; compatible with caution or alternative agent.
pediatric: Safety and efficacy in pediatric patients not established.
geriatric: Higher plasma levels due to reduced first-pass clearance; start with 150 mg twice daily.
renal: No primary dosage adjustment required in mild to moderate renal disease; monitor ECG.
hepatic: Dose must be reduced by 50% in hepatic cirrhosis due to saturable first-pass metabolism.
advantages: Dual Class IC sodium blockade and mild beta-adrenergic blockade provides built-in AV nodal protection against 1:1 flutter
Proven oral 'pill-in-the-pocket' option for terminating acute episodes of atrial fibrillation at home
Extended-release formulation enables convenient twice-daily dosing
disadvantages: Characteristic metallic taste in the mouth
Non-linear pharmacokinetics make dose titration unpredictable
Strictly contraindicated in heart disease and asthma
key_points: Safe only in hearts free of prior heart attacks or weakness (structurally normal hearts)
Leaves a strange metallic taste in the mouth that is harmless; take with meals
memory_trick: PROPA-fenone: Prototypic IC sodium blocker; Propranolol-like beta-blockade; Avoid In Asthma & Infarct; Metallic taste.

description: A non-iodinated benzofuran derivative of amiodarone designed to reduce multiorgan thyroid and pulmonary toxicities, used to maintain sinus rhythm in paroxysmal or persistent atrial fibrillation.
mechanism_of_action: Exhibits multichannel antiarrhythmic activity across all four Vaughan Williams classes (blocks IKr, IKs, INa, ICa, and possesses non-competitive antiadrenergic activity); lacks the iodine moieties of amiodarone and incorporates a methane-sulfonyl group to reduce lipophilicity.
pharmacodynamics: Reduces sinus heart rate, slows AV nodal conduction, prolongs myocardial refractory periods, and reduces cardiovascular hospitalizations and mortality in patients with non-permanent atrial fibrillation (ATHENA trial).
absorption: Poorly absorbed in fasting state (bioavailability approx. 4%); food dramatically increases absorption to approx. 15% (must be taken with morning and evening meals).
distribution: Apparent volume of distribution approx. 1400 L; highly bound to human plasma proteins (>98%), predominantly albumin.
metabolism: Extensively metabolized in the liver by CYP3A4 to an active N-debutyl metabolite (approx. 1/10th the potency of dronedarone).
excretion: Excreted predominantly in faeces (approx. 84%) via biliary elimination; approx. 6% excreted in urine as metabolites; zero unchanged drug in urine.
half_life: 25 to 30 hours (substantially shorter than amiodarone's 50-day half-life)
onset: Steady state reached within 4 to 8 days
duration: 12 hours (dosed 400 mg twice daily with meals)
indications: Reduction of the risk of cardiovascular hospitalization in patients with paroxysmal or persistent atrial fibrillation who are currently in sinus rhythm or who will be cardioverted (ATHENA trial)
contraindications: PERMANENT ATRIAL FIBRILLATION (PALLAS trial: doubled mortality, stroke, and HF hospitalizations)
NYHA Class IV heart failure or NYHA Class II-III heart failure with recent decompensation (ANDROMEDA trial: doubled mortality)
Second- or third-degree AV block or sick sinus syndrome without a functioning pacemaker
Severe hepatic impairment
Concurrent use of strong CYP3A inhibitors or QT-prolonging drugs
warnings: Black box warning: STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED in patients with symptomatic heart failure or permanent atrial fibrillation (PALLAS and ANDROMEDA trials showed significant excess mortality)
Hepatotoxicity: rare cases of acute liver failure requiring transplantation (monitor liver enzymes)
Increases serum creatinine by approx. 0.1 mg/dL by inhibiting tubular secretion (OCT2) without reducing actual GFR
Pulmonary toxicity: rare cases of interstitial lung disease / pneumonitis
serious_adverse_effects: Severe worsening of heart failure / cardiac death (in decompensated HF or permanent AF)
drug_interactions: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, clarithromycin - strictly contraindicated)
Dabigatran (P-gp inhibition increases dabigatran levels; reduce dabigatran dose or avoid)
Digoxin (doubles digoxin levels; reduce digoxin dose by 50%)
Statins (simvastatin/atorvastatin - doubles statin levels; reduce statin dose)
monitoring: Liver function tests (ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase) prior to initiation, monthly for 6 months, then periodically
ECG at baseline and every 3-6 months (verify patient remains in sinus rhythm and has not progressed to permanent AF)
Serum creatinine (expect benign 0.1 mg/dL increase; verify baseline GFR)
pregnancy: Category X; strictly contraindicated in pregnancy due to embryotoxicity and fetal teratogenicity.
lactation: Excretion in human milk unknown; breastfeeding strictly contraindicated.
pediatric: Safety and efficacy in children under 18 years not established.
geriatric: No primary dose adjustment; monitor heart failure symptoms and ensure sinus rhythm.
renal: No dosage adjustment required in renal impairment (cleared predominantly by liver).
hepatic: Contraindicated in severe hepatic impairment; monitor liver enzymes closely.
advantages: Lacks the iodine moieties of amiodarone, drastically reducing thyroid toxicity, pulmonary fibrosis, and corneal deposits
Shorter half-life (30 hours vs. 50 days) allows rapid clearance if side effects occur
Proven in the ATHENA trial to reduce cardiovascular hospitalizations and death in paroxysmal AF
disadvantages: LETHAL in permanent atrial fibrillation or heart failure (PALLAS and ANDROMEDA trials)
Low oral bioavailability (15%) and must be taken with full meals twice daily
key_points: ONLY for intermittent (paroxysmal) atrial fibrillation; NEVER take if AF has become permanent
Always take 400 mg twice daily with your morning and evening meals
memory_trick: DRONE-darone: De-iodinated amiodarone; Reduces hospitalizations in Non-permanent AF; Deadly in permanent AF.

description: An endogenous purine nucleoside with an ultra-short half-life (<10 seconds) that transiently blocks AV nodal conduction, serving as the gold standard acute rescue agent for paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT).
strengths: 3 mg/mL (2 mL vial = 6 mg, 4 mL vial = 12 mg)
dosage_forms: Solution for Rapid IV Bolus Injection
mechanism_of_action: Binds to myocardial purinergic A1 receptors coupled to Gi proteins, activating inward rectifier potassium channels (IK-Ado) and inhibiting adenylate cyclase-mediated L-type calcium influx; profoundly slows AV nodal conduction velocity and prolongs AV refractory periods.
pharmacodynamics: Terminates re-entrant circuits traversing the AV node (AVNRT and AVRT / Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome) within 10 to 30 seconds; produces coronary arteriolar vasodilation via A2A receptors (utilized in cardiac stress testing).
absorption: Administered exclusively by rapid intravenous push; not active orally.
distribution: Rapidly taken up into erythrocytes and vascular endothelial cells by nucleoside transporters; volume of distribution approx. 10 L.
metabolism: Rapidly metabolized intracellularly by adenosine deaminase (ADA) to inosine, and phosphorylated by adenosine kinase to AMP; not dependent on hepatic CYP450 enzymes.
excretion: Eliminated within seconds; metabolites are degraded to uric acid and excreted in urine.
half_life: Less than 10 seconds (cellular uptake and enzymatic breakdown occur in under 10 seconds)
onset: Immediate (within 10 to 20 seconds of rapid push)
indications: Acute conversion of paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT) including AVNRT and AVRT to sinus rhythm
Diagnostic unmasking of underlying atrial flutter or atrial fibrillation by transiently blocking AV conduction
Pharmacologic myocardial perfusion stress imaging (vasodilator stress agent via A2A receptors)
contraindications: Second- or third-degree AV block or sick sinus syndrome (in patients without a functioning pacemaker)
Severe active bronchospasm, bronchial asthma, or severe COPD (can trigger bronchospasm via A2B/A3 receptors)
Known hypersensitivity to adenosine
Pre-excited atrial fibrillation (Wolff-Parkinson-White with AF - risk of 1:1 ventricular conduction and VF)
warnings: ADMINISTRATION TECHNIQUE IS CRITICAL: Half-life is <10 seconds; MUST be administered as an ultra-rapid IV push over 1 to 2 seconds directly into a large proximal vein (antecubital fossa), IMMEDIATELY followed by a rapid 20 mL normal saline flush
Warn the awake patient beforehand of intense transient chest tightness, facial flushing, and impending doom (lasts 10-20 seconds)
Continuous multi-lead ECG monitoring and resuscitation equipment must be at the bedside
common_adverse_effects: Intense chest pressure / dyspnea (frightening to patient, lasts 15 seconds)
Transient sinus bradycardia / asystole on ECG (lasts 2 to 5 seconds)
serious_adverse_effects: Prolonged asystole / ventricular standstill requiring CPR
Atrial fibrillation or ventricular fibrillation precipitation
drug_interactions: Theophylline, aminophylline, caffeine (adenosine receptor antagonists: competitive inhibition blocks adenosine effect; requires higher adenosine doses)
Dipyridamole (nucleoside uptake inhibitor: potentiates adenosine 4-fold; reduce adenosine dose to 3 mg)
Carbamazepine (potentiates AV block; reduce dose)
monitoring: Continuous ECG rhythm strip recording during and for 5 minutes after injection
Blood pressure and heart rate
SpO2 and respiratory status
pregnancy: Category C; safe during pregnancy for maternal SVT due to ultra-short 10-second half-life and zero fetal exposure.
lactation: Zero infant exposure due to 10-second maternal clearance; compatible with breastfeeding.
pediatric: Approved for pediatric PSVT (initial dose: 0.1 mg/kg rapid IV push, maximum 6 mg; second dose 0.2 mg/kg, max 12 mg).
geriatric: Higher incidence of sinus pause and bradycardia; start with 6 mg rapid push.
renal: No dosage adjustment required in renal failure (eliminated by ubiquitous cellular enzymes).
hepatic: No dosage adjustment required in hepatic disease.
advantages: Gold standard first-line medication for terminating acute SVT with a 90-95% success rate within 30 seconds
Ultra-short half-life (<10 seconds) ensures any adverse side effects disappear in less than a minute
Safe in pregnancy and across pediatric age groups
disadvantages: Must be given as a rapid proximal IV slam with a 20 mL saline flush, or it degrades before reaching the heart
Produces terrifying transient chest tightness, flushing, and brief asystole (warn the patient)
key_points: Administer as an ultra-fast IV push into the elbow vein, instantly followed by a 20 mL saline flush
Warn the patient: 'You will feel intense chest tightness for 15 seconds, but it will pass quickly'
memory_trick: ADENO-sine: Arrests AV Node; Ultra-short half-life (<10s); Rapid IV slam; Saline flush needed; Asthmatics beware.

description: An orally active Class IB antiarrhythmic and structural analogue of lidocaine, used for life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias, myotonic disorders (non-dystrophic myotonia), and neuropathic pain.
mechanism_of_action: Inhibits fast inward voltage-gated sodium channels (Nav1.5 in myocardium, Nav1.4 in skeletal muscle), shortening action potential duration and effective refractory period in Purkinje fibers; accelerates repolarization and blocks persistent/late sodium currents (INa-late).
pharmacodynamics: Suppresses abnormal ventricular automaticity and triggered activity without depressing cardiac output; in skeletal muscle, blocks hyperactive sodium channels, dramatically relieving muscle stiffness in non-dystrophic myotonia.
absorption: Rapidly and almost completely absorbed (>90%); peak plasma concentrations in 2 to 3 hours; food does not impair total absorption.
distribution: Widely distributed into tissues and crosses the blood-brain barrier; volume of distribution approx. 5 to 7 L/kg; 50-60% bound to plasma proteins.
metabolism: Extensively metabolized in the liver (approx. 90%) by CYP2D6 and CYP1A2 to inactive hydroxy and hydroxymethyl metabolites.
excretion: Excreted in urine (approx. 10% as unchanged drug; remainder as metabolites); renal clearance increases in acidic urine (pH < 5) and decreases in alkaline urine.
half_life: 10 to 12 hours (prolonged to 20-25 hours in severe liver failure or heart failure)
indications: Documented life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias (sustained ventricular tachycardia)
Non-dystrophic myotonia (myotonia congenita and paramyotonia congenita - FDA/EMA orphan drug of choice)
Long QT syndrome type 3 (LQT3 - selectively blocks late sodium current)
Refractory diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain (second-line)
contraindications: Preexisting second- or third-degree AV block without a functioning pacemaker
Cardiogenic shock
Known hypersensitivity to mexiletine or local anesthetics of the amide type
warnings: Narrow therapeutic window: therapeutic plasma range is 0.5 to 2.0 mcg/mL (toxicity common above 2.0 mcg/mL)
Neurotoxicity: fine tremor, ataxia, nystagmus, dizziness, and paresthesias are early signs of toxicity
Gastrointestinal distress: take with food or antacids to minimize nausea and heartburn
Drug-induced liver injury / DRESS syndrome
common_adverse_effects: Tremor (fine hand tremor - common dose-limiting sign)
serious_adverse_effects: DRESS syndrome (Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms)
drug_interactions: CYP2D6 / CYP1A2 inducers (phenobarbital, phenytoin, rifampin - decrease mexiletine levels by 50%)
CYP2D6 inhibitors (fluoxetine, quinidine - elevate mexiletine levels, precipitating toxicity)
Cigarette smoking (induces CYP1A2, increasing mexiletine clearance)
Caffeine (mexiletine inhibits caffeine metabolism, causing caffeine jitters)
monitoring: Serum mexiletine trough concentrations (therapeutic target: 0.5 to 2.0 mcg/mL)
Neurological assessment for tremor, ataxia, or nystagmus at every visit
Baseline and periodic 12-lead ECG
Liver function tests
pregnancy: Category C; use during pregnancy only if potential benefit justifies potential risk.
lactation: Excreted in breast milk in concentrations higher than maternal plasma; breastfeeding not recommended.
pediatric: Approved in children for non-dystrophic myotonia and congenital LQT3 (weight-based dosing: 2-8 mg/kg/day divided TID).
geriatric: Increased susceptibility to neurological toxicity and dizziness; start at lowest dose (150 mg twice daily).
renal: No dosage adjustment required in mild to moderate renal disease; in severe renal failure (CrCl < 10 mL/min), reduce dose.
hepatic: Dose must be reduced by 50% in severe hepatic cirrhosis (clearance is heavily liver-dependent).
advantages: Orally bioavailable equivalent to IV lidocaine, allowing chronic outpatient therapy for ventricular arrhythmias
First-line orphan drug of choice for relieving severe muscle stiffness in myotonia congenita
Specific targeted efficacy in Long QT syndrome type 3 (LQT3) by blocking late sodium current
disadvantages: Narrow therapeutic window with high rate of neurological side effects (hand tremors, ataxia, dizziness)
Requires dosing 3 times daily with food to prevent gastric irritation
key_points: Oral cousin of lidocaine used for heart rhythm disturbances and muscle stiffness
Always take with food or milk to prevent stomach upset; report hand tremors immediately
memory_trick: MEXI-letine: Modern Equivalent of eXtended-oral Lidocaine; Invaluable for Myotonia; Tremor signals Toxicity.

description: The quintessential Class IB antiarrhythmic and amide local anesthetic, administered intravenously for acute ventricular arrhythmias during myocardial infarction or cardiac arrest, and topically for regional anesthesia.
mechanism_of_action: Binds to the intracellular pore of voltage-gated fast sodium channels (Nav1.5) in cardiac tissue, preferentially binding to open and inactivated channels in depolarized, ischemic, or rapidly firing myocardium; shortens action potential duration and effective refractory period.
pharmacodynamics: Suppresses abnormal ventricular automaticity and re-entrant circuits in ischemic myocardium without depressing AV nodal conduction or cardiac contractility; topically blocks sodium channels in sensory nerve fibers, producing reversible local anesthesia.
absorption: Negligible oral bioavailability (<3%) due to massive hepatic first-pass metabolism; administered parenterally or topically.
distribution: Rapidly distributes into well-perfused organs (brain, heart, liver), followed by muscle and fat; volume of distribution approx. 1.5 L/kg; 60-80% bound to plasma alpha-1 acid glycoprotein.
metabolism: Extensively metabolized in the liver (>95%) by CYP3A4 and CYP1A2 to active de-ethylated metabolites (monoethylglycinexylidide - MEGX, and glycinexylidide - GX) which possess convulsant and antiarrhythmic properties.
excretion: Excreted in urine (approx. 90% as metabolites; less than 5% as unchanged parent drug).
half_life: 1.5 to 2 hours (prolonged to 4-10 hours in heart failure, cardiogenic shock, or severe hepatic disease)
duration: 10 to 20 minutes after single IV bolus; requires continuous infusion
indications: Acute treatment of ventricular tachycardia (VT) and ventricular fibrillation (VF) during cardiac arrest (alternative to amiodarone)
Ventricular arrhythmias complicating acute myocardial infarction or cardiac surgery
Local and regional infiltration anesthesia, peripheral nerve blocks, and epidural anesthesia
Post-herpetic neuralgia (5% lidocaine transdermal patch)
Topical anesthesia of mucosal membranes
contraindications: Severe sinoatrial, atrioventricular, or intraventricular heart block without pacemaker
Stokes-Adams syndrome or Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome
Known hypersensitivity to amide-type local anesthetics
warnings: LOCAL ANESTHETIC SYSTEMIC TOXICITY (LAST): Accidental intravenous injection during nerve block or excessive infusion causes CNS toxicity (circumoral numbness, tinnitus, metallic taste, seizures) followed by cardiovascular collapse; treat immediately with 20% INTRAVENOUS LIPID EMULSION
Hepatic clearance is blood-flow dependent: drastically reduce maintenance infusion rate in heart failure, cardiogenic shock, or cirrhosis
Narrow therapeutic window: therapeutic serum levels 1.5 to 5.0 mcg/mL (toxic > 5.0 mcg/mL)
common_adverse_effects: Circumoral paresthesias (tingling around lips and tongue - warning sign of toxicity)
drug_interactions: Beta-blockers (propranolol/metoprolol decrease hepatic blood flow, increasing lidocaine levels and toxicity)
Cimetidine (inhibits CYP3A4, increasing lidocaine levels)
Amiodarone (additive myocardial depression and neurotoxicity)
monitoring: Continuous ECG telemetry and automated blood pressure monitoring during IV infusion
Serum lidocaine levels if infusion exceeds 24 hours (therapeutic range: 1.5 to 5.0 mcg/mL)
Monitor mental status for early neurotoxicity (tinnitus, slurred speech, confusion)
pregnancy: Category B; widely used for epidural and infiltration anesthesia in labor and delivery with excellent safety.
lactation: Excreted in breast milk in low levels; compatible with breastfeeding.
pediatric: Approved in pediatric resuscitation (1 mg/kg IV/IO initial bolus, followed by 20-50 mcg/kg/min infusion).
geriatric: Lower volume of distribution and reduced hepatic clearance; decrease initial bolus and maintenance infusion by 50%.
renal: No dosage adjustment for initial bolus; metabolites accumulate in severe renal failure with prolonged infusion (>24h).
hepatic: Reduce maintenance infusion rate by 50% in severe hepatic disease or cardiogenic shock (decreased liver perfusion).
advantages: Rapid onset within 60 to 90 seconds for acute ventricular arrhythmias in the ICU or cardiac arrest
